title: Costs: serverless, databases and AI spend
summary: The three meters running under every AI app (functions, database, tokens), what makes each one jump, and the limits and alerts that stop a surprise bill.
youWillLearn: How serverless hosting, a database plan and an AI API each count what you owe
Why AI tokens are usually the meter that runs fastest
Three cheap fixes: a smaller model, an output cap, and not asking twice
Which spend limits and alerts to set on day one, and who should pay the bill

glossary.serverless function: Code that runs only when a request arrives, on servers the host manages. You pay per use, not per machine.
glossary.invocation: One run of a serverless function, triggered by one request.
glossary.egress: Data sent out of a service to the internet or your app. Many providers bill for it after a free amount.
glossary.quota: The amount of something a plan includes before extra charges or limits start.
glossary.token: The unit AI models read and write in, roughly a short word or part of a word. AI APIs bill per token.
glossary.input tokens: The tokens you send to the model: instructions, the note, any history.
glossary.output tokens: The tokens the model writes back. They cost several times more per token than input tokens.
glossary.max_tokens: A setting on each AI request that caps how many output tokens the model may write.
glossary.spend limit: A hard ceiling on what a provider may charge you in a period. Past it, requests are refused or the service pauses.
glossary.budget alert: An email or message sent when spending passes a threshold you chose, like 50% of the monthly budget.

steps.title: Notely's three monthly bills
body: Notely's 5,000 users reach the app server, Notely's code running on Vercel. It keeps notes in the database, run by Supabase, and asks the Claude API, Anthropic's AI, for summaries.
Each of the three sends you a bill every month. Today they are small, and nobody has set any limit on them.

scene.caption: Three services behind Notely, each with its own bill.

steps.title: The invoice that ruins a good month
body: A popular newsletter mentions Notely. Great week. Then the invoices arrive, and the AI bill is thirty times last month's. Hosting tripled too.
Popularity was only part of it. A screen Claude Code wrote asks for a new summary every time a note is opened, even when the note has not changed. Nobody set a limit, so nothing stopped it.
changes: ~ 5,000 users → 20,000 users
~ App Server → Claude API: a new summary on every note open
~ Hosting bill $20 → $60

scene.caption: More users, and far more AI calls per user.

steps.title: Three meters under every AI app
body: Most small AI apps pay three kinds of bills, and each counts something different.

Hosting counts requests and compute time. The database charges a monthly plan, plus extras past what it includes. The AI API counts tokens, on every single call. Know what each meter counts, and you know what makes it spin.

callout.text: A flat with three meters: electricity, water, gas. Leave one tap running all night and only that bill explodes. You need to know which tap.

changes: ~ App Server, Database, Claude API: each shows what its meter counts

steps.title: Serverless: pay per run
body: Notely's app server is really a set of serverless functions: code that runs only when a request arrives. You pay per invocation (one run), for compute time and memory, and for data sent out.
No traffic costs almost nothing; a spike scales the bill with it. AI calls are slow, so waiting time matters too.

callout.text: Check how your host counts the seconds a function spends waiting on Claude. Some bill the whole time it is open, others mostly active work. A summary that takes 20 seconds can cost far more under one billing style than the other.

changes: ~ App Server in focus: billed per run and per second
~ Database and Claude API step back

scene.caption: The hosting meter: every request starts a short, billed run.

steps.title: Databases: a plan, then extras
body: Supabase and most hosted databases sell a monthly plan with a quota: database size, compute size (the size of the machine), file storage and egress, the data sent out.
Bills jump when you outgrow one, often from a query that loads every row, logs or AI outputs piling up, or a bigger compute size nobody scaled back.

callout.text: You met indexing and caching in system design. Here they also save money: fewer rows read means less compute and less egress.

changes: ~ Database in focus: a plan, then extras past its quota
~ App Server and 20,000 users step back

scene.caption: The database meter: a flat plan until you outgrow it.

steps.title: AI: you pay for every token
body: AI APIs bill per token, roughly a short word. Input tokens are what you send: instructions plus the whole note. Output tokens are what Claude writes, and cost several times more each.
Three levers: a smaller model for simple jobs like summaries, a max_tokens cap on output, and trimming what you send.

code.caption: Log res.usage on every call (lesson 4). That is your cost per feature, per user.

changes: ~ Claude API in focus: a smaller model, output capped
~ Database steps back

scene.caption: The AI meter: each call is cheaper, but there are still too many.

steps.title: The cheapest call is the one you skip
body: Notely's bug was asking the same question twice. An unchanged note has the same summary. So save the summary with a fingerprint of the note text, and only call Claude when the text changes.
Then add a daily limit per user, so one account or script cannot run up the bill alone.

code.caption: Status 429 means "too many requests". Reopening an unchanged note now costs nothing on the AI meter.

changes: ~ Database: keeps each summary with the note's fingerprint
~ App Server → Claude API: only when the note changed
~ App Server: at most 20 summaries per user a day
~ AI bill $500 → $60

scene.caption: Saved summaries come from the database; Claude is asked only about changed notes.

steps.title: Limits and alerts on day one
body: A bug or a leaked key can still spend money overnight. So set guardrails at every provider.

A budget alert emails you at, say, 50% and 80% of the monthly budget. A spend limit is a hard ceiling. Check what Anthropic, Vercel and Supabase each offer. Then decide: is a paused feature worse than a big bill?

callout.text: For client builds, create the hosting, database and AI accounts in the client's name, with the client's card. You stay an invited member. The bill, the limits and the data belong to them.

changes: + You: get an email when spending passes 50% and 80%
~ Claude API: a hard spend limit is set
~ Spend limits None → Set

scene.caption: A ceiling on the AI bill, and an early warning to you.

steps.title: Runaway loops spend while you sleep
body: The scariest bills come from code that calls the AI in a loop. A browser screen that re-asks every time it redraws. Retries with no cap. An agent that keeps calling tools. A key in browser code that someone else finds.
Each runs at machine speed, all night. That is exactly what limits are for.

code.caption: useEffect runs code after React draws the screen. With no dependency list it runs after every redraw, and each new summary causes another. Add one, and keep the server-side check too.

callout.text: Search the code for every AI call (messages.create). Is each one on the server, behind a login? Does it set max_tokens? Is there a per-user limit and a saved result? Are retries capped? Does any useEffect fetch without a dependency list?

changes: − 20,000 users
+ Browser: one open tab re-asking for a summary nonstop
~ App Server: flooded by that one tab
~ Claude API: the spend limit is hit, extra calls refused

scene.caption: One looping tab hammers the app; the spend limit stops the bill.

steps.title: Recap: know the meters, cap them
body: Hosting counts runs and compute time, the database counts plan quotas, and the AI API counts every token. AI is usually the fastest meter.
Pick a smaller model, cap max_tokens, and never ask the same question twice. Then set alerts and spend limits at every provider, in the client's name for client work.
changes: ~ Browser: loop fixed, one request per note
~ App Server, Database, Claude API: calm again

scene.caption: Three meters, each watched and capped.

quiz.question: Notely's AI bill doubled, but the number of users did not change. What is the most likely cause to check first?

options.text: The database plan quietly got more expensive.
options.why: That would show on the database invoice, not on the AI bill.

options.text: More AI calls per user, like re-summarizing unchanged notes or a loop.
options.why: Same users but more tokens means each user triggers more or bigger calls. Logged token usage per request will show where.

options.text: Serverless functions are slower this month.
options.why: Slower functions raise the hosting bill, not the per-token AI bill.

quiz.question: Which change cuts the cost of each summary without changing how often summaries happen?

options.text: A smaller model and a max_tokens cap.
options.why: A smaller model costs less per token, and the cap limits the expensive output tokens. Each call gets cheaper.

options.text: Moving the Claude call into the browser.
options.why: The tokens cost the same wherever the call starts, and your API key would be exposed to everyone.

options.text: A bigger serverless function memory size.
options.why: More memory can make hosting more expensive. It does not change what Claude charges.

quiz.question: You are handing over a client's salon booking app. Whose card should the Claude, Vercel and Supabase accounts use?

options.text: Yours, and you add a markup to your monthly invoice.
options.why: It can work as a service, but you carry the risk of a runaway bill, and the client does not own their accounts or data.

options.text: The cheapest free tiers, so there is no card at all.
options.why: Free tiers have limits that can pause a live business app, and often no backups. Fine for a demo, risky for a salon taking bookings.

options.text: The client's, with spend limits and alerts set, and you as an invited member.
options.why: The client owns the bill and the data, the limits protect them, and you keep the access you need to support the app.

takeaways: Three meters: hosting (runs and compute time), database (plan quotas), AI (every token).
Output tokens cost more than input. Use a smaller model where it is good enough, and always set max_tokens.
The cheapest AI call is the one you skip: save results and only regenerate when the input changes.
Set budget alerts and spend limits at every provider on day one.
For client work, accounts and cards belong to the client. You are an invited member.
